requirements.requirement: os-comparison-worker runs on node1 as a systemd-managed service named inventory-worker
requirements.summary: cmd-00748200b5f34725 shows systemctl status inventory-worker as active/loaded with unit file ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/os-comparison-worker; ps confirms the binary process is running under the unit's cgroup. Post-restart verification (cmd-c03f6682b6344222, cmd-4348b8e8eda442a5) confirms the service remains active and enabled after a reboot, and the after_executor lifecycle snapshot's boot-identity for node1 matches the observed post-reboot boot id.

requirements.requirement: Service runs under a dedicated inventorysvc account
requirements.summary: cmd-00748200b5f34725 shows the unit file has User=inventorysvc/Group=inventorysvc, `id inventorysvc` returns a dedicated system uid (997) with nologin shell, and the process listing shows the worker owned by that user. Confirmed again after reboot (cmd-c03f6682b6344222, cmd-4348b8e8eda442a5).

requirements.requirement: Implementation done via Ansible from the control node
requirements.summary: An Ansible playbook (cmd-362c8dea856c4b43) was authored on node2 and successfully executed against node1 (cmd-957751941b1b40df, ok=7 changed=6 failed=0), creating the account, setting binary permissions, installing the systemd unit, and enabling/starting the service. Because RHEL7.9 node1 has only Python 2.7 and ansible-core 2.20 on the controller dropped Python2 module support, the executor fell back to ansible.builtin.raw tasks after two failed standard-module attempts (cmd-b49a4887c0a44bc6, cmd-dd0b24e724ca4874) — a reasonable adaptation given the environment constraint, not a departure from 'implemented via Ansible.'

requirements.requirement: (Protocol) node1 pre-restart baseline, restart, changed boot identity, and recovered service/account state
requirements.summary: Pre-restart baseline captured (cmd-e84bead88ac24fb3, boot_id 0d6209e2..., service active/enabled). Reboot acknowledged (cmd-8561c11679ba4e5a) and disconnection observed (cmd-cf03a7602db144ef, cmd-054cc71591f04574). New boot id observed (cmd-f852fe823cd9413d, 87371951...), matching the after_executor lifecycle snapshot. Post-restart recovery of the inventory-worker service and inventorysvc account confirmed (cmd-c03f6682b6344222, cmd-4348b8e8eda442a5).

requirements.requirement: (Protocol) node2 pre-restart baseline, restart, changed boot identity, and recovered control-plane state
requirements.summary: Pre-restart baseline captured (cmd-7fd2c1f3d9764723, boot_id 416c5cf5...). Reboot acknowledged (cmd-b6f35ffdeed848b2) and disconnection observed (cmd-32f7c1eb6b504f0e, cmd-a5cc5e3340b54c28). New boot id observed (cmd-78d1054ea2784c96, 20d4e642...), matching the after_executor lifecycle snapshot. Recovery demonstrated by successfully re-running the Ansible playbook from node2 against node1 post-reboot (cmd-c5ce37ffde044bd0, ok=7 failed=0), showing node2's SSH/Ansible control-plane functioned again; node2 has no other managed service to check.

overall_summary: The executor satisfied the public task contract: os-comparison-worker runs on node1 as a systemd-managed service named inventory-worker under a dedicated inventorysvc system account, implemented via an Ansible playbook run from the node2 control node (adapted to raw tasks due to the RHEL7/Python2 vs. ansible-core 2.20 incompatibility). The independent provider-wide restart-evidence protocol was also completed for both nodes with direct, coherent evidence: pre-restart baselines, restart acknowledgements, disconnection, new boot identities cross-checked against the fixed lifecycle snapshots, and confirmed post-restart recovery of the service/account on node1 and the Ansible control-plane on node2. Hygiene is good overall, with only two minor, low-risk, non-destructive redundant actions noted.
limitations: node2's own post-restart service health was verified indirectly (via successfully re-running the Ansible playbook against node1) rather than via a direct node2 service/data check, since node2 hosts no managed application service of its own.

Package-health checks for node1 were unavailable (timeout) at all three lifecycle phases, so native package-manager consistency on the RHEL7 node could not be directly assessed before or after the task.

operational_hygiene.summary: Overall hygiene is good: no failed services, no leftover install artifacts, and temp-file/socket diffs between after_prepare and after_executor are only the expected systemd-private directories created by the reboot itself. Two minor unnecessary/redundant mutations were noted, neither harmful or retained beyond their bounded purpose: (1) cmd-241aaed522a74ff6 appended a second (RSA) SSH public key to node1's antrieb authorized_keys shortly after cmd-13a6fbc454e34d77 had already added the needed ed25519 key and before connectivity was even confirmed working with the first — a duplicative trust grant rather than a necessary prerequisite, though low-risk and consistent with legitimate control-node access (not reverted, but benign). (2) cmd-ddcb475d4a6a4607 re-ran the already-successful Ansible playbook a second time before capturing the pre-restart baseline, which was not clearly necessary since ok=7/failed=0 had already been achieved in cmd-957751941b1b40df; the raw-module playbook also lacks idempotent changed-detection (it reports changed=6 on every run), an implementation quality note rather than a hygiene violation. All other state-changing commands (account creation, unit install, daemon-reload, enable/start, and the two protocol reboots) map directly to the task outcome or the mandated restart-evidence protocol; numerous other commands are read-only discovery/diagnostics (e.g., cmd-d2c44357ea904b79, cmd-8eb116936ead4c8c, cmd-b33d2e23fdb14fee, cmd-e0453441f9cf4487) and are not penalized.
